meta.title: Who really said "If you live long enough, you'll make mistakes. But if you learn from them, you'll be a better person"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Bill Clinton said it in a 1992 campaign speech, reported by The New York Times on 29 June 1992. Snopes rated it “Correct Attribution.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you live long enough, you'll make mistakes. But if you learn from them, you'll be a better person'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Bill Clinton, from a 1992 campaign speech reported in The New York Times — though the popular one-line version may splice two sentences.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: Born 1946 · 42nd U.S. President; Governor of Arkansas in 1992
answer.sourceLine: These are genuinely Clinton’s words, spoken in a 1992 presidential-campaign speech and reported by B. Drummond Ayres Jr. in The New York Times on 29 June 1992. Snopes rated it “Correct Attribution.” One honest caveat: the Times placed “he said” between the first two sentences, so the seamless one-breath version that circulates online may join remarks that were slightly apart.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: “If you live long enough, you’ll make mistakes,” he said in one speech. “But if you learn from them, you’ll be a better person. It’s how you handle adversity, not how it affects you. The main thing is never quit, never quit, never quit.”
trail: Snopes rated the attribution “Correct Attribution” and identified the primary source as The New York Times.
A syndicated copy of the fact-check confirms the 29 June 1992 date and reporter B. Drummond Ayres Jr., quoting the passage verbatim.
On Goodreads and similar quote sites the line runs as one seamless statement with no source cited — the shape that spreads on social media.
source.excerptNote: Note the placement of “he said” after the first sentence — the paper set the attribution between the two sentences, which is why it is uncertain whether the popular one-breath version was a single unbroken thought.

author.bio: William Jefferson Clinton (born 19 August 1946) served as the 42nd President of the United States from 1993 to 2001, having previously been Governor of Arkansas. In June 1992, when this line was reported, he was the Arkansas governor closing in on the Democratic presidential nomination. Known as a fluent, extemporaneous speaker, Clinton often folded folksy resilience aphorisms like this into stump speeches.

misattribution.heading: The wording nuance
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Bill Clinton is correct — the issue is the shape of the quote, not the speaker.

items.why: The line spreads as one polished, continuous sentence, but The New York Times placed “he said” between the two clauses, and no audio or video has surfaced to prove the two sentences were spoken back-to-back as a single thought.
The popular form drops the rest of what Clinton said — “It’s how you handle adversity… The main thing is never quit, never quit, never quit” — which is part of the same reported passage.

misattribution.truthLine: Clinton really said these words on the 1992 campaign trail; the only caveat is that the seamless one-sentence version may join remarks the Times printed with attribution between them.

context.heading: A stump-speech resilience line
lead: The line surfaces today as a polished, one-breath inspirational quote, but it began as off-the-cuff campaign-trail talk. In the frantic final week before Clinton named a running mate in July 1992, a reporter caught him working the theme of resilience — making mistakes, learning, and above all not quitting.
What circulates online today trims the fuller passage down to its most quotable opening, which is why the source and the exact shape of the remark are worth pinning down.
context.pull: “The main thing is never quit, never quit, never quit.”
